metadata.title: Firm training, automation, and wages: International worker-level evidence

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses OECD PIAAC microdata (2012 wave for the international analysis; 2012 and 2017 for the United States; 2012 and 2015 for Germany) and restricts the analytic sample to workers aged 25–65 who have information on both workplace task measures (to construct automation risk) and log hourly wages. For the main international regressions, the authors apply entropy balancing weights (ebalance in Stata) to reweight the control group so that covariate moments match the treated group; they also report that columns (1)–(4) use weights that give each country the same weight, while column (5) uses entropy-balancing weights. The manuscript does not report a specific PIAAC sampling weight variable name (e.g., TOTWGT), but it does describe the use of entropy balancing and country-equal weighting, and it relies on PIAAC’s representative sampling design for cross-country inference. In the Germany panel fixed-effects model (Table 5), the notes state that observations are not weighted, indicating a deliberate omission of weights in that robustness specification.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible Values are not applicable because the dependent variables are not PV-based cognitive achievement scores; the outcomes are an automation-risk index derived from task-use items and log hourly wages, plus standardized digital skills. Missing-data handling is implemented through complete-case restriction for the main automation-risk and wage regressions (requiring non-missing automation risk and wages), while digital-skills analyses use additional sensitivity imputations due to optional assessment.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: International analysis: uses PIAAC pooled data across 37 industrialized countries (excluding the Russian Federation; treating England and Northern Ireland as the United Kingdom) and restricts to employees aged 25–65 with information on both automation risk (constructed from workplace task-use items) and log hourly wages. Occupation coding is at two-digit ISCO level where available; for Austria, Canada, Estonia, and Finland, only one-digit occupation/industry codes are available in the PIAAC Public Use File, so one-digit fixed effects are used there. For the main automation-risk and wage regressions, the authors explicitly state that the sample is restricted to respondents without missing information on both automation risk and wages; they also note similar results in a more complete sample including missing wage information. Digital-skills analyses further restrict to participants with digital skills information (digital skills were optional and only administered after a computer core test), and robustness analyses impute missing digital skills using multiple imputation-like scenarios (zero/global minimum/country minimum) and also consider an indicator for participation in the digital assessment.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIAAC 2012 (international pooled; adult workers 25–65), automation risk from workplace task use
top_predictors: Firm training (job-related training in prior 12 months)
main_findings.performance_metrics: OLS with entropy balancing (Table 2, column 5): Firm training coefficient = −0.0377 (SE 0.0023), p<0.01; R²=0.24; Observations=91,470. Interpretation in text: 3.8 percentage-point reduction; ~1/5 SD; 8% of mean automation risk.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIAAC 2012 pooled data (37 countries; employees aged 25–65) and constructing individual automation risk from workplace task-use items, the study leveraged firm training, occupation fixed effects, and numeracy skills (with entropy balancing reweighting) to predict automation risk, finding that firm training reduced automation risk by 3.8 percentage points (coefficient −0.0377). This indicates that expanding employer-provided training can lower workers’ susceptibility to automation, suggesting a policy focus on incentivizing and supporting on-the-job upskilling rather than only targeting unemployed workers, though the cross-sectional design means causality cannot be fully established.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIAAC 2012 (international pooled; adult workers 25–65), log hourly wages
top_predictors: Firm training (job-related training in prior 12 months)
main_findings.performance_metrics: OLS with entropy balancing (Table 7, column 5): Firm training coefficient = 0.0713 (SE 0.0058), p<0.01; R²=0.38; Observations=91,470. Interpretation in text: ~7.1% wage increase; adding automation risk reduces the wage effect by ~15% (Table 7, column 6).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIAAC 2012 pooled data (37 countries; employees aged 25–65) and modeling log hourly wages, the study leveraged firm training, occupation fixed effects, and numeracy skills with entropy balancing to predict wages, finding that firm training increased wages by about 7.1% (coefficient 0.0713). This indicates that employer training is associated with meaningful labor-market payoffs and that part of these gains is linked to reduced automation risk, supporting policies that encourage training aligned with technological change, while recognizing that unobserved selection may still remain despite reweighting and fixed effects.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIAAC 2012 (international pooled; adult workers 25–65), digital skills (standardized)
top_predictors: Firm training (job-related training in prior 12 months)
main_findings.performance_metrics: OLS with entropy balancing (Table 6, column 5): Firm training coefficient = 0.0481 (SE 0.0089), p<0.01; R²=0.59; Observations=72,180. Text interpretation: +0.048 SD; baseline sample without imputing missing digital skills treated as lower bound.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIAAC 2012 pooled data (37 countries; employees aged 25–65 with digital-skills information) and modeling standardized digital skills, the study leveraged firm training, numeracy skills, and occupation fixed effects with entropy balancing to predict digital skills, finding that firm training increased digital skills by 0.048 standard deviations (coefficient 0.0481). This indicates that training likely helps workers adapt to technology by improving digital competencies, suggesting that training policy should include technology-relevant components, while noting that digital-skills assessment is optional and missingness is handled via lower-bound sample restriction and sensitivity imputations.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses OECD PIAAC microdata to examine whether employer-provided firm training reduces workers’ automation risk and improves wages. The main international analysis pools 37 countries using the 2012 wave and constructs an individual-level automation risk index (0–1) from PIAAC workplace task-use items, then estimates OLS models with country/industry/occupation fixed effects and entropy balancing reweighting to address selection into training. In the preferred specification (Table 2, column 5), firm training reduces automation risk by 3.8 percentage points (coefficient −0.0377; R²=0.24; N=91,470). In the wage model (Table 7, column 5), firm training increases log hourly wages by 7.1% (coefficient 0.0713; R²=0.38; N=91,470), and adding automation risk reduces the wage effect by about 15% (Table 7, column 6). Digital skills analyses (Table 6, column 5) show a +0.048 SD increase (N=72,180), interpreted as a mechanism, with the caveat that digital skills were optional and missingness is handled via lower-bound restriction and sensitivity imputations.
